title: Watcher, ladder, routing and backstop

story: Wednesday, 14:10. Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, is on step 2 of RH-1234, writing the test for the empty card. The test times out. Nova reads the component again and runs the test again: timeout. Again. An hour later it has run the same test forty times, every turn has gone through the gateway, our service that adds the Anthropic key and counts the cost, and been billed, and nothing has changed. Nobody noticed, because a run in our platform may take as long as it needs: there is no turn limit, no time limit and no budget limit.

A limit would have stopped this loop. But it would also have stopped the run next to it, which is slow because it is careful: it reads twenty files and runs the whole suite before every change. From the outside, both runs look equally busy.
hook.question: How does the platform tell a run going in circles from a run that is slow but useful, and what does it do about the loop without throwing the work away?

p: Counting tool calls, turns or minutes measures activity, and both runs in the story are very active. What separates them is progress, so the harness, our program inside the VM that runs the Claude session, counts that instead. Three things count as real progress: a check that failed before now passes, an item of the plan is marked done, or the agent reads a file it has not read before, which means it learned something new. Running a test again, editing a file or reading the same file again is activity, not progress.

The progress watcher is a hook in the harness, registered for PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure, so it sees every tool call and its result, as you saw in the lesson about hooks. It keeps one number, flatFor: how many tool events in a row brought no progress. Any real progress sets it back to 0. The careful run reads new files and turns failing checks green, so its counter keeps falling back to zero; the looping run's counter only goes up. The verdict goes into the run's state and into every heartbeat, so the orchestrator, our Temporal worker that follows the run, can see it too.

notes.text: Normalized: timestamps and temp paths are removed and numbers in errors masked, so two runs of the same command look the same.
No clock and no turn count anywhere: only progress moves this number.
A check passing is progress only if it failed before. A test that was always green proves nothing new.

deeper.h: Go deeper: check-ins, and one line far away
p: Time is still measured, just never used to stop anything. When a run passes twice its own estimate from the plan, Nova posts a three-line check-in in the ticket's thread, what is taking time and why it is worth it, and continues; again at four and eight times. Only a Stop from a person ends a run that is working.

Behind the watcher sits a cost backstop, set far above what a normal ticket costs (later about three times the 99th percentile of successful runs). It reads the run's spend from the gateway at step boundaries only, never in the middle of a turn. For the first four weeks it runs in shadow mode: it only counts the runs it would have paused. After that it may pause a run between turns, save a checkpoint and ask in the thread with Continue and Stop buttons; Continue resumes the same session exactly where it was.

A flat counter says that something is wrong; it does not say what. So the watcher also looks for four patterns that agents fall into, the same ones OpenHands, an open-source coding agent, checks for in its stuck detector. The same command with the same result, three times in a row. The same error again, three times, recognised by its error signature: the first line of the error with every number masked, so "Timeout of 5002 ms" and "Timeout of 5004 ms" count as one error. Undo and redo: an edit brings a file back to a state it had before. And ping-pong: two actions taking turns, A-B-A-B-A-B.

The name matters because it goes directly into the first nudge the agent reads, and good advice depends on the right diagnosis. "You ran the same command three times" is useful when the agent repeats itself, but it is the wrong advice for an agent that alternates between two edits. That is also why the order and the exact wording of the rules matter, as you will see in the lab.

notes.text: Three in a row. Counted anywhere in the last six, this rule would also match A-B-A-B-A-B, and the ping-pong rule below could never answer.
ev.error is already the signature, with numbers masked.
Even positions all the same action, odd positions all the same other action.

read.h: The ladder: change the approach, one rung at a time
p: A loop is a reason to change the approach, not to kill the run. So when flatFor keeps growing, the harness acts, one rung at a time, and each rung is cheap. After 6 tool events without progress it nudges: a short message that names the loop and asks for a different approach. After 9 it asks the agent to stop and write a short new plan for the step. Both happen inside the turn: the watcher's hook returns additionalContext, text the model reads together with the tool result.

The next three rungs happen between turns, at a step boundary, after a checkpoint, so nothing is lost. After 12 the step is re-run one effort level higher, which is the routing rule below. After 15 the harness checkpoints, ends the session and starts a fresh one from notes.md, so a context full of failed attempts is thrown away but the work is not. After 18 it asks a person in the ticket's thread, with what was tried and the evidence, and from then on the waiting rules for questions apply. Any real progress resets the ladder, and a review finding that returns after a "fix" goes directly to the last rung.

notes.text: Starting values. The watcher logs verdicts on real runs, and the numbers are tuned from those logs.
Index 2 is think_harder: the first rung that lives between turns.
Counted as ai_agents_watcher_handoffs_total{rung}, for the alerts and the weekly run review.

deeper.h: Go deeper: which model, how much effort, and thinking harder
p: Effort is how much work the model puts into an answer: low, medium, high or xhigh. A routing table in the harness gives each kind of job a model and an effort: planning and building use Opus 5.5 at medium, the readiness check Sonnet 5.5 at low, read-only helpers Haiku 5.5 at medium, QA Sonnet 5.5 at medium, and the CI fixer Opus 5.5 at low, because CI itself is the checker. In Anthropic's tests, Opus at medium with only the failed attempts re-run at high was both cheaper and better than running everything at high.

So when a step's checks fail, the harness re-runs that step once, one level higher, in the same session: it changes the effort with applyFlagSettings at the step boundary instead of starting a new session, so the prompt cache stays warm: the provider keeps the start of the conversation ready, which makes the next calls much cheaper. The output limit is 64,000 tokens, never a tight one that cuts long answers, and a test fails the build if anyone ever adds maxTurns, maxBudgetUsd or taskBudget to the session options.

lab.title: Catch the loop, not the slow run
lab.goal: Feed recorded tool events from four runs to a small progress watcher and ladder on your laptop, and make it act on the loop while leaving the slow, healthy run alone.

guess.q: A run fails a test, edits the file, fails again with a different message, edits again, and the test passes. Six tool events. With a ladder that nudges after 6 events without progress, does it nudge?

options.text: Yes: six tool calls happened, and none of them finished the ticket
options.why: That counts activity. The test that failed and now passes is real progress, and it sets the counter back to 0.

options.text: No: the counter rises to 4 and drops to 0 when the failing test passes
options.why: Failing, editing and failing again are not progress, but the pass is. The healthy loop never reaches 6.

options.text: No: the watcher only looks at runs that are older than an hour
options.why: The watcher has no clock at all. It only counts events without progress.

follow.say: Make a folder. This lab needs no packages: the watcher is plain JavaScript, fed with recorded events.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/g3-14 && cd ~/academy-labs/g3-14
npm init -y > /dev/null && npm pkg set type=module

follow.say: Save four recorded runs on RH-1234: a healthy one, a flaky test retried again and again, an edit that is undone and redone, and two commands taking turns.
Save the watcher. loopKind and rememberFile are done; progressed counts every tool call as progress, which is the mistake you will see first.
Save the ladder and a script that feeds one recorded run to the watcher and prints what the ladder would do after each event.
Feed it the flaky run, because that is the loop from the story.
follow.see:
#  event                                   flat  loop
 1  Bash npm test -- ProjectsTable (fail)       0  -
 2  Read src/ProjectsTable.tsx                  0  -
 3  Bash npm test -- ProjectsTable (fail)       0  -
…
20  Read src/ProjectsTable.tsx                  0  -
(twenty events, the counter never moves, and the ladder never steps in: activity looks like progress)

lab.build: Write progressed(ev) in watcher.mjs, following its comment: a check that is in this.failing and now passes (remember to add failing checks to the set and remove passing ones), a TodoWrite event with todoCompleted, or a Read of a file that is not yet in this.seen (add it). Then run node run.mjs healthy and node run.mjs flaky again, and compare the two.
checks: node run.mjs healthy never shows a counter above 4 and prints no rung line.
In node run.mjs flaky, event 1 has flat 1 (a failing test is not progress) and event 2 has flat 0 (the first read of the file is).
node run.mjs flaky prints five rungs in order: nudge at event 8, replan at 11, think_harder at 14, fresh_start at 17 and ask_person at 20.
node run.mjs undo shows undo and redo at event 6, and after the fix below its nudge names undo and redo.
After the fix below, node run.mjs pingpong shows ping-pong at event 6 and its nudge says ping-pong.
lab.fix: Run node run.mjs pingpong. The agent alternates git stash and git stash pop, but the nudge says "same command, same result", which tells it to stop repeating one command, the wrong advice. The ping-pong rule never answers. Find out why: the same-command rule counts matching events anywhere in the last six, and A-B-A-B-A-B already contains A three times. Make that rule mean what its name says, three in a row (last.slice(-3) all equal to ev.key). Then pingpong ends with ping-pong, undo with undo and redo, and flaky with same error again.
explain: Why does reading a new file count as progress, but reading the same file again does not?
Why do the first two rungs happen inside the turn, and the last three only at a step boundary after a checkpoint?
Why is a limit on turns or time the wrong tool for catching the loop in the story?
lab.done: The healthy run is never touched, the flaky run climbs all five rungs, and every loop gets its right name.

check.q: A careful run reads twenty new files and runs the whole test suite before each change, so it uses many tool calls per step. Will the ladder act?

options.text: Yes, after 6 tool calls in a step
options.why: The counter counts events without progress, not tool calls. First reads and newly passing checks keep setting it back to 0.

options.text: No, because reading new files and turning failing checks green is real progress
options.why: That is the point of measuring progress: a slow, useful run is never punished.

options.text: Yes, once it passes twice its estimate
options.why: Passing the estimate only posts a check-in. Nothing stops or nudges the run because of time.

check.q: The watcher has seen 12 tool events without progress. What happens next?

options.text: The run is stopped and the ticket goes back to the requester
options.why: The ladder never stops a run. Even the last rung only asks a person a question.

options.text: A person is asked in the thread right away
options.why: Asking a person is the last rung, at 18. There are cheaper things to try first.

options.text: At the next step boundary, the step is re-run one effort level higher in the same session
options.why: Rung 3, think harder. It happens between turns, after a checkpoint, so nothing is lost.

check.q: Why does the platform not set maxTurns or a budget limit to catch loops?

options.text: A limit stops slow but useful runs in the middle of their work, and throws that work away
options.why: The watcher catches the loop by its lack of progress, and the far backstop only pauses between turns, after a checkpoint.

options.text: The Agent SDK has no such options
options.why: It has them. We choose not to use them, and a test fails if anyone adds one.

options.text: Limits would make the prompt cache cold
options.why: The cache has nothing to do with it. The reason is the work a limit would throw away.

p: The watcher is harness/src/watcher.ts, registered for PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure; its verdict goes into the run state and the heartbeats. The ladder is harness/src/ladder.ts and counts ai_agents_watcher_handoffs_total{rung}. The routing table and rerunOneLevelUp are harness/src/routing.ts, with CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=64000 and a 1-hour prompt cache for runs that wait on people (5 minutes for routines), and test/no-limits.test.ts guards against maxTurns, maxBudgetUsd and taskBudget. The check-ins and the backstop are harness/src/backstop.ts, with NOVA_BACKSTOP_MODE=shadow for the first four weeks and spend read from the gateway's per-run endpoint.

Two things to fix while you build: in the G3-32 sketch the same-command rule counts matches anywhere in the last six events, so the ping-pong rule can never fire; make it three in a row as in this lesson. And applyFlagSettings for changing effort on a running query must be checked against the current SDK docs, together with the cache-read rate in the first spike.

tickets.why: The progress watcher: what counts as progress, and the four loop patterns.
The ladder: nudge, re-plan, think harder, fresh start, ask a person.
The routing table, one effort level up on failed checks, and no limits on the session.
Check-ins past the estimate and the far cost backstop, first in shadow mode.

words.plain: A hook that sees every tool call and counts only real progress: a fixed check, a plan item done, a first read.
How many tool events in a row brought no progress. Real progress sets it back to 0.
The first line of an error with numbers masked, so repeats of one error look the same.
Five cheap steps when progress stays flat: nudge, re-plan, think harder, fresh start, ask a person.
How much work the model puts into an answer: low, medium, high or xhigh.
A cost line far above a normal ticket where a run pauses between turns and asks; shadow mode first.

review.q: From memory: the three kinds of real progress and the four loop patterns.
review.a: A check that failed now passes, a plan item done, a first read. Same command and result three times in a row, the same error three times, undo and redo, ping-pong.

review.q: Why does the first nudge name the loop, and what goes wrong when it names the wrong one?
review.a: Good advice needs the right diagnosis. "You ran the same command three times" helps an agent that repeats itself but misleads one that alternates between two actions, which is why the same-command rule must mean three in a row, so that ping-pong can be named.

review.q: A run passes twice the estimate in its plan. What does Nova do, and what does time never do in our platform?
review.a: Nova posts a three-line check-in in the thread (what takes time and why it is worth it) and continues, again at four and eight times. Time never stops or nudges a run; only a person's Stop ends a run that is working.

remember: Measure progress, not activity, and when progress stops, change the approach one cheap rung at a time instead of killing the run.
